title: Fabric IQ Ontology: From OneLake Data to Shared Business Meaning
purpose: Show how an ontology's logical vocabulary (entity types, properties, relationships) binds to real OneLake data and materializes as a queryable instance graph that data agents, Power BI, and apps all query through the same governed meaning.
accessibleSummary: An architecture flow: a modeler declares entity types, properties, and relationships as a logical vocabulary layer. A data-binding layer maps that vocabulary onto real OneLake sources — lakehouse tables, eventhouse streams, and semantic models — carrying schema-evolution rules, quality checks, and provenance. The bindings materialize into a queryable instance graph, a dependent Fabric item built on Graph in Microsoft Fabric that requires a tenant setting to be enabled. NL2Ontology translates natural-language questions into structured queries constrained to the published ontology's definitions, and the ontology layer routes execution to whichever backend actually holds the data. Data agents, Power BI, and apps all consume the same materialized graph. A warning node flags that upstream data changes are not automatically reflected — the graph needs an explicit refresh.
longDescription: This is a layered architecture flow, not a straight pipeline: the logical vocabulary layer (entity types, properties, relationships) is authored independently of any single data source, then bound to concrete OneLake data through a separate data-binding layer that maps columns to properties and keys to relationship links. That binding materializes into an instance graph — a distinct, dependent Fabric item built on Graph in Microsoft Fabric, storing actual nodes and edges with lineage, not a virtual view computed on the fly, and it requires the tenant's Graph capability to be enabled before it works. Two branches feed from there: NL2Ontology takes a natural-language business question and translates it into a structured query constrained to the ontology's published definitions (units, join paths, validity windows), while the ontology layer itself routes any query's execution down to whichever backend actually holds the data — GQL against Graph, KQL against Eventhouse. Both data agents and Power BI/apps consume the resulting graph, sharing one definition of what a 'customer' or 'shipment' means instead of each redefining it. A warning node captures a genuine architectural gap: upstream source changes are not automatically reflected in the bound data or graph and require an explicit manual or scheduled refresh.

nodes.label: OneLake data (lakehouse, eventhouse, semantic model)
nodes.summary: The concrete data an ontology binds to — lakehouse tables, eventhouse streams, and Power BI semantic models.
nodes.detail: OneLake underlies Fabric IQ as the unifying data layer across clouds and on-premises sources, using shortcuts, mirroring, and the OneLake catalog so the same governed data grounds semantic models, ontologies, and agents. An ontology's data binding attaches to lakehouse tables, eventhouse streams, or Power BI semantic models sitting on this shared substrate.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because every source is already on OneLake, an ontology doesn't require a separate data-movement step to bind to it — the same governed data that reports and pipelines already use is what the ontology maps its vocabulary onto.

evidence.note: OneLake underlies Fabric IQ as the unifying layer across clouds and on-premises sources, using shortcuts, mirroring, and the OneLake catalog so the same governed data grounds semantic models, ontologies, and agents.

inputs: Lakehouse Delta tables, Eventhouse KQL streams, and Power BI semantic models already registered in OneLake
processing: Data lands and is governed on OneLake through normal ingestion, mirroring, or shortcut mechanisms
No ontology-specific movement or copy step occurs at this stage
outputs: A set of queryable OneLake sources available for an ontology's data-binding layer to map onto
drill.example: A retailer's order and shipment lakehouse tables, already used by existing Power BI reports, become the source data an ontology later binds its Order and Shipment entity types to — with no new copy of the data created.
controls: Which OneLake sources are exposed for ontology binding
Existing OneLake security and governance controls apply unchanged
failureModes: Assuming ontology binding requires a data export or duplication step it does not

nodes.label: Entity types, properties, relationships
nodes.summary: The logical vocabulary layer: reusable business concepts with facts and typed connections, defined above any single table.
nodes.detail: An ontology is composed of entity types (the things), properties (their facts), and relationships (how they connect), together with constraints and rules that keep those representations consistent across teams. An entity type is a reusable logical model of a real-world concept — deliberately elevated above any single table so inconsistent per-source column definitions don't fragment the concept's meaning. Relationships are typed, directional links that can carry their own attributes (distance, confidence, effective-at) and cardinality rules.
nodes.whyItMatters: Elevating the vocabulary above any single table is what lets the same 'Customer' concept stay singular even when three different source systems define a customer row differently — the fragmentation problem lives in the binding layer, not the vocabulary.

evidence.note: An ontology in Fabric IQ is composed of entity types (the things), properties (their facts), and relationships (how they connect), together with constraints and rules that keep those representations consistent across teams.

An entity type is a reusable logical model of a real-world concept, deliberately elevated above any single table so that inconsistent per-source column definitions don't fragment the concept's meaning.
Relationships are typed, directional links between entity types or instances that can carry their own attributes (distance, confidence, effective-at) and cardinality rules.

inputs: Business requirements for the concepts and relationships an organization needs to reason about
processing: Declare entity types (e.g. Customer, Order, Shipment) with their standardized names, identifiers, and constraints
Declare properties as the facts each entity type carries
Declare typed, directional relationships between entity types, including their own attributes and cardinality rules
outputs: A logical vocabulary — entity types, properties, relationships — independent of any single data source
drill.example: A Shipment entity type declares a 'delivers-to' relationship to a Customer entity type and a 'contains' relationship to Order, each carrying its own effective-at attribute, before any data binding is attached.
controls: Naming and constraint conventions for entity types, so the same concept isn't redeclared under different names
Which properties and relationships are mandatory vs optional for a given entity type
failureModes: Declaring near-duplicate entity types for the same real-world concept because teams didn't coordinate
Under-specifying cardinality rules, allowing relationship data that violates the intended business rule

nodes.label: Data binding layer
nodes.summary: Maps the logical vocabulary onto real OneLake sources — columns to properties, keys to relationships.
nodes.detail: Data binding connects an ontology's entity types, properties, and relationships to concrete OneLake data — lakehouse tables, eventhouse streams, or Power BI semantic models — by mapping columns to properties and keys to relationship links, while carrying schema-evolution rules, data-quality checks, and provenance at the concept level.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the layer that actually resolves the 'same concept, different columns per source' problem: the vocabulary stays singular while the binding absorbs per-source variation, and it's also where schema-evolution and data-quality rules live so the graph doesn't silently break when a source table changes.

evidence.note: Data binding connects an ontology's entity types, properties, and relationships to concrete OneLake data — lakehouse tables, eventhouse streams, or Power BI semantic models — by mapping columns to properties and keys to relationship links, while carrying schema-evolution rules, data-quality checks, and provenance at the concept level.

inputs: Concrete OneLake lakehouse tables, eventhouse streams, or semantic models to bind against
processing: Map source columns to declared properties
Map source keys to declared relationship links
Attach schema-evolution rules, data-quality checks, and provenance metadata at the concept level
outputs: A concept-level mapping from vocabulary to concrete data, ready to materialize into an instance graph
drill.example: The Customer entity type's 'email' property is bound to a CustomerEmail column in one lakehouse table and to a different column name in a mirrored CRM source, with both bindings resolving to the same standardized property.
controls: Which source is authoritative when the same property is bound from multiple sources
Data-quality checks enforced at bind time (e.g. required fields, format checks)
failureModes: Binding a property to a source column whose meaning has silently drifted, without a data-quality check catching it
No provenance tracking, making it hard to trace an instance graph value back to its source row

nodes.label: Ontology instance graph
nodes.summary: A materialized, queryable graph of entity instances and relationship edges, built on Graph in Microsoft Fabric.
nodes.detail: The ontology graph is a queryable instance graph — nodes as entity instances, edges as asserted or derived links with metadata — built on top of the separate Graph in Microsoft Fabric item, which must be enabled as a tenant setting before an ontology's graph features work. An entity instance is a concrete, timestamped occurrence of an entity type populated from a data binding; it retains which source created it and when it was true.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is a materialized, dependent Fabric item — not a virtual view computed at query time — so its freshness is a real operational concern (see the refresh warning) rather than something that's automatically always current.

evidence.note: The ontology graph is a queryable instance graph — nodes as entity instances, edges as asserted or derived links with metadata — built on top of the separate Graph in Microsoft Fabric item, which must be enabled as a tenant setting before an ontology's graph features work.
An entity instance is a concrete, timestamped occurrence of an entity type populated from a data binding; it retains which source created it and when it was true.

inputs: The concept-level data binding mapping from the previous stage
processing: Populate entity instances (nodes) from bound source rows, timestamped and provenance-tagged
Populate relationship edges from bound relationship links, carrying their declared attributes
Persist nodes and edges as a dependent Fabric item on top of Graph in Microsoft Fabric
outputs: A materialized, queryable instance graph — the concrete node/edge structure that NL2Ontology and routed queries traverse
drill.example: The Shipment-to-Customer 'delivers-to' relationship materializes as an edge between a specific Shipment instance and a specific Customer instance, timestamped to when that delivery relationship was true.
controls: Whether Graph in Microsoft Fabric is enabled as a tenant setting (a prerequisite)
Refresh cadence for keeping the graph in sync with bound source changes
failureModes: Attempting to use ontology graph features before Graph in Microsoft Fabric is enabled at the tenant level
Treating the graph as always-current when it is a materialized snapshot — see the refresh warning node

nodes.label: Warning: no automatic refresh
nodes.summary: Upstream source changes are not automatically reflected — the graph needs an explicit manual or scheduled refresh.
nodes.detail: Upstream data source changes — new, updated, or deleted rows — are not automatically reflected in an ontology's bound data or graph. They require an explicit manual or scheduled refresh of the graph model before they become visible to queries or agents reading it.
nodes.whyItMatters: A team that assumes the instance graph is always current risks agents and reports answering from stale business state — this is a real operational gap that must be planned for with an explicit refresh schedule, not an edge case.

evidence.note: Upstream data source changes (new, updated, or deleted rows) are not automatically reflected in an ontology's bound data or graph — they require an explicit manual or scheduled refresh of the graph model before they become visible.

inputs: An instance graph populated from a data binding at some point in time
Upstream source data that has since changed (new, updated, or deleted rows)
processing: Detect that the source has changed since the last graph materialization
Trigger a manual or scheduled refresh of the graph model
Re-materialize affected nodes and edges from the current bound data
outputs: An updated instance graph reflecting current source state, or a stale graph if refresh was skipped
drill.example: A shipment is marked delivered in the source lakehouse table, but an operations agent querying the ontology graph before the next scheduled refresh still sees it as in-transit, because the graph is a materialized snapshot, not a live view.
controls: Explicit refresh schedule for the graph model, sized to how time-sensitive the concept is
Monitoring for refresh failures so staleness doesn't go unnoticed
failureModes: Agents or reports acting on stale graph state believing it is live
No alerting on refresh failures, so staleness compounds silently over multiple missed cycles

nodes.label: NL2Ontology
nodes.summary: Translates a natural-language business question into a structured query constrained to the ontology's definitions.
nodes.detail: NL2Ontology converts natural-language business questions into structured ontology queries and constrains the generated filters, joins, units, and validity windows to the definitions published in the ontology, rather than letting a model infer them freely from raw schema.
nodes.whyItMatters: Constraining generation to the published ontology definitions is what prevents an LLM from inventing a join path or unit conversion that happens to look plausible but doesn't match governed business meaning — the same trap that makes raw NL2SQL over ungoverned schema risky.

evidence.note: NL2Ontology converts natural-language business questions into structured ontology queries and constrains the generated filters, joins, units, and validity windows to the definitions published in the ontology, rather than letting a model infer them freely from raw schema.

inputs: The published ontology's entity types, properties, relationships, and constraints
processing: Parse the question against the ontology's vocabulary rather than raw table schema
Generate a structured query constrained to the ontology's declared filters, joins, units, and validity windows
Pass the structured query to ontology query routing for execution
outputs: A structured, ontology-constrained query ready to execute against the instance graph
drill.example: "Which shipments to customers in the cold-chain program were delayed last week?" is translated into a structured traversal of the Shipment-to-Customer relationship filtered by the ontology's declared 'cold-chain program' property and validity window, rather than a raw guess at table joins.
controls: Which ontology is the target for a given natural-language surface (a data agent, Copilot, an app)
Fallback behavior when a question references a concept not present in the ontology
failureModes: A question referencing a concept outside the published ontology producing a poor or unanswerable translation instead of a clear refusal
Treating NL2Ontology as infallible and skipping human review for high-stakes generated queries

nodes.label: Federated query routing
nodes.summary: Routes a business-level query to whichever backend actually holds the data — GQL against Graph, KQL against Eventhouse.
nodes.detail: Ontology queries start from an entity type and let a caller filter by property, traverse relationships, and aggregate over time using business terminology; the ontology layer then routes execution to whichever backend holds the data, such as GQL for Graph in Microsoft Fabric or KQL for Eventhouse.
nodes.whyItMatters: The caller writes one business-level query without needing to know or care whether the underlying data lives in the graph store or an eventhouse — the ontology layer is what makes that engine choice invisible.

evidence.note: Ontology queries start from an entity type and let a caller filter by property, traverse relationships, and aggregate over time using business terminology; the ontology layer then routes execution to whichever backend holds the data, such as GQL for Graph in Microsoft Fabric or KQL for Eventhouse.

inputs: A structured, ontology-level query (from NL2Ontology or authored directly)
processing: Determine which backend holds the data for the entity types and properties referenced
Translate the ontology-level query into the backend's native query language (GQL for Graph, KQL for Eventhouse)
Execute against the appropriate backend and return results in ontology terms
outputs: Query results expressed in business-level ontology terms, regardless of which backend actually executed them
drill.example: A query traversing Shipment-to-sensor-reading relationships is routed to KQL against the bound Eventhouse data, while a query traversing Customer-to-Order relationships is routed to GQL against Graph — both expressed identically to the caller as ontology traversals.
controls: Which backend is authoritative when an entity type's data binding spans multiple backends
failureModes: Cross-backend queries (e.g. joining a graph-bound entity with an eventhouse-bound entity) performing poorly if the routing layer can't push down efficiently

nodes.label: Fabric data agent
nodes.summary: A conversational agent grounded in the ontology, answering natural-language questions with consistent business meaning.
nodes.detail: A Fabric data agent is described as a virtual analyst connected to Fabric data sources that answers natural-language questions for a specific domain, grounded in semantic models and ontologies, and publishable across Microsoft 365, Foundry, Copilot Studio, and custom apps.
nodes.whyItMatters: Grounding the agent in the ontology rather than raw schema is what gives it the same consistent 'customer' and 'shipment' meaning across every surface it's published to, instead of redefining those concepts per deployment.

evidence.note: A Fabric data agent is described as a virtual analyst connected to Fabric data sources that answers natural-language questions for a specific domain, grounded in semantic models and ontologies, and publishable across Microsoft 365, Foundry, Copilot Studio, and custom apps.

inputs: A user's natural-language question submitted through a published surface (Microsoft 365, Foundry, Copilot Studio, a custom app)
The ontology's NL2Ontology-translated, routed query results
processing: Submit the question through NL2Ontology and routed query execution
Assemble a natural-language answer grounded in the returned, ontology-governed data
outputs: A conversational answer consistent with the same business definitions used by every other ontology consumer
drill.example: A supply-chain analyst asks a data agent embedded in Teams "which shipments are at risk this week," and the agent's answer traces the same Shipment/Customer ontology definitions a Power BI report built independently also uses.
controls: Which ontology(ies) and data sources a given agent is scoped to
Publishing surface and authentication mode for the agent
failureModes: An agent scoped to stale or unrefreshed graph data giving confidently wrong answers (see the refresh warning)

nodes.label: Power BI & applications
nodes.summary: Reports and custom apps querying the same ontology, sharing one definition of business concepts with agents.
nodes.detail: Power BI semantic models and custom applications consume the same materialized instance graph and routed query layer as data agents, so a report's 'customer' means exactly what an agent's 'customer' means — both trace back to the same entity-type vocabulary and data binding.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the governance payoff of the whole architecture: business terms and KPIs stay consistent across reports, agents, and applications instead of being redefined per experience.

evidence.note: Ontologies in Fabric IQ can be generated or aligned directly from Power BI semantic models already in production, so business terms and KPIs stay consistent across reports, agents, and applications instead of being redefined per experience.

inputs: Routed query results from the ontology layer
Power BI report authoring or custom application logic
processing: Query the ontology's instance graph through the same routing layer data agents use
Present results in a report or application UI
outputs: Reports and applications whose business terms match every other ontology consumer exactly
drill.example: A Power BI report and a data agent both surface 'total at-risk shipments this week,' and because both trace to the same ontology definition of 'at-risk,' the two numbers agree without manual reconciliation.
controls: Which ontology a given report or app is bound to
Access governance on who can query which entity types
failureModes: A report built against raw tables instead of the ontology silently diverging from an agent's ontology-grounded answer for the same business question

walkthrough.title: 1. Start: data already governed on OneLake
walkthrough.explanation: Lakehouse tables, eventhouse streams, and semantic models sitting on OneLake are the concrete data an ontology will bind its vocabulary to — no separate copy step needed.

walkthrough.title: 2. Declare the vocabulary independently of any table
walkthrough.explanation: Entity types, properties, and relationships are defined as reusable business concepts, deliberately elevated above any single source's column definitions.

walkthrough.title: 3. Bind the vocabulary to real data
walkthrough.explanation: Columns map to properties, keys map to relationship links, carrying schema-evolution rules, quality checks, and provenance at the concept level.

walkthrough.title: 4. Materialize the instance graph
walkthrough.explanation: Bindings populate a queryable graph of entity instances and relationship edges — a real, persisted Fabric item built on Graph in Microsoft Fabric, not a virtual view.

walkthrough.title: 5. Warning: refresh is not automatic
walkthrough.explanation: Upstream source changes don't propagate to the graph on their own — an explicit manual or scheduled refresh is required, a real operational gap to plan for.

walkthrough.title: 6. Translate natural language into a governed query
walkthrough.explanation: NL2Ontology constrains generated filters, joins, units, and validity windows to the published ontology, rather than letting a model infer them from raw schema.

walkthrough.title: 7. Route to whichever backend holds the data
walkthrough.explanation: The same business-level query executes as GQL against Graph or KQL against Eventhouse — the caller never has to know which.

walkthrough.title: 8. Data agents answer with governed meaning
walkthrough.explanation: A conversational agent grounded in the ontology answers questions with the same business definitions everywhere it's published.

walkthrough.title: 9. Power BI and apps share the same definitions
walkthrough.explanation: Reports and applications query the identical ontology layer, so 'customer' and 'shipment' mean the same thing whether a human or an agent is asking.
